(a) Authority To Transfer Items in Stockpile.—
        (1) In general.—Notwithstanding section 514 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (22 U.S.C. 2321h), the President is authorized to transfer to the Republic of Korea, on such conditions as the President may determine, any or all of the items described in paragraph (2). 
        (2) Covered items.—The items referred to in paragraph (1) are munitions, equipment, and materiel such as tanks, trucks, artillery, mortars, general purpose bombs, repair parts, barrier material, and ancillary equipment if such items are—
            (A) obsolete or surplus items; 
            (B) in the inventory of the Department of Defense; 
            (C) intended for use as reserve stocks for the Republic of Korea; and 
            (D) as of the date of the enactment of this Act, located in a stockpile in the Republic of Korea or Japan.  
        (3) Valuation of concessions.—The value of concessions negotiated pursuant to paragraph (1) shall be at least equal to the fair market value of the items transferred, less any savings (which may not exceed the fair market value of the items transferred) accruing to the Department of Defense from an avoidance of the cost of removal of such items from the Republic of Korea or of the disposal of such items. The concessions may include cash compensation, services, waiver of charges otherwise payable by the United States (such as charges for demolition of United States-owned or United States-intended munitions), and other items of value.   
        (4) Termination.—No transfer may be made under the authority of this subsection after the date that is three years after the date of the enactment of this Act.  
    (b) Certification Regarding Materiel in Stockpile.—Not later than 60 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Defense shall certify to the appropriate committees of Congress whether or not the ammunition, equipment, and materiel in the War Reserves Stockpile for Allies, Korea that are available for transfer to the Republic of Korea is of any utility to the United States for any of the following:
        (1) Counterterrorism operations. 
        (2) Contingency operations. 
        (3) Training. 
        (4) Stockpile, pre-positioning, or war reserve requirements.  
    (c) Termination of Stockpile.—
        (1) In general.—At the conclusion of the transfer to the Republic of Korea under subsection (a) of items in the War Reserves Stockpile for Allies, Korea pursuant to that subsection, the War Reserves Stockpile for Allies, Korea program shall be terminated.   
        (2) Disposition of remaining items.—Any items remaining in the War Reserves Stockpile for Allies, Korea as of the termination of the War Reserves Stockpile for Allies, Korea program under paragraph (1) shall be removed, disposed of, or both by the Department of Defense.   
    (d) Appropriate Committees of Congress Defined.—In this section, the term “appropriate committees of Congress” means—
        (1) the Committees on Armed Services, Appropriations, and Foreign Relations of the Senate; and 
        (2) the Committees on Armed Services, Appropriations, and International Relations of the House of Representatives.

fable.w: The tempting reading treats the certification requirement and the negotiated concessions with the Republic of Korea as participation. The certification goes to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. The concessions are the terms of a transfer transaction with a foreign government, not consultation with outside parties before a federal decision. Nothing in the section provides for public comment, a hearing, an advisory body, rulemaking, or a right to sue.
fable.s: the Secretary of Defense shall certify to the appropriate committees of Congress

qwen_block.w: The section authorizes the President to transfer items to the Republic of Korea and requires the Secretary of Defense to certify findings to Congress. The Republic of Korea is an outside entity, but the text does not require consultation, coordination, or participation by the ROK in the decision-making process; it simply grants authority to transfer items to them. The certification is directed to Congress, which is inside the federal government. Therefore, there is no required participation by outside parties in the federal decision.
qwen_block.s: the Secretary of Defense shall certify to the appropriate committees of Congress whether or not the ammunition, equipment, and materiel in the War Reserves Stockpile for Allies, Korea that are available for transfer to the Republic of Korea is of any utility to the United States

opus.w: The only formal interaction that resembles procedure is a certification to congressional committees, and Congress is inside the federal government, so that is not participation. The concessions negotiated with the Republic of Korea are an exchange with the party receiving the transfer. Korea is not being consulted on a federal decision. No comment period, hearing, outside advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue is created.
opus.s: the Secretary of Defense shall certify to the appropriate committees of Congress whether or not the ammunition, equipment, and materiel in the War Reserves Stockpile for Allies, Korea that are available for transfer to the Republic of Korea is of any utility to the United States
opus.b: **Tempting misreading:** The President negotiates "concessions" with the Republic of Korea, which is outside the U.S. federal government. The Secretary of Defense also must "certify to the appropriate committees of Congress." Both look procedural. But Korea is the other party to a deal, receiving the items and paying for them. Bargaining over a transfer price is not the same as being consulted on a federal policy decision. The certification goes to Congress, which is inside the federal government. No public comment, hearing, outside advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue appears anywhere in the section.

qwen_chat.w: The section authorizes the President to transfer items to a foreign government but does not require consultation or coordination with that foreign government or any other outside party in making the decision. The President determines the conditions unilaterally. The only reporting requirement is to Congress, which is inside the federal government.
qwen_chat.s: the President is authorized to transfer to the Republic of Korea, on such conditions as the President may determine
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the transfer of items to the Republic of Korea involves coordination with a foreign government, which is outside the U.S. federal government. However, the statute authorizes the President to determine the conditions and does not require consultation, coordination, or participation by the Republic of Korea in the decision-making process itself. The Republic of Korea is the recipient, not a participant in the federal decision. The only external interaction mentioned is a certification to Congress, which is inside the federal government.
